title: Pass segment_reduce args as a tuple, not a set, in test_pytorch_scatter_test_cases
body: `test_pytorch_scatter_test_cases` builds the positional arguments of `torch._segment_reduce` as a set literal, `{x, reduce}`, then unpacks it with `*`. A set has no order: whether the tensor or the reduce string comes first depends on their hashes, so the call can receive the string as data and fail with `TypeError: segment_reduce(): argument 'data' (position 1) must be Tensor, not str`. A tuple keeps the intended order.

title: [MPS] Migrate `addc[mul|div]` to Metal
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.18.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198753
* #198743
* __->__ #196924

Follows the precedent set by lerp and clamp: both ops now register `addc{mul,div}_stub` and run through the shared `exec_ternary_kernel`, which gains an alpha flavor for the `value` scalar so the family covers `clamp`, `lerp`, `addcmul` and `addcdiv` alike.

Fixes the same cast error lerp had: the `_cast_` ternary kernels were instantiated for the output dtype, so an `out=` wider than the common dtype widened the computation as well. They now compute at the iterator's common dtype and cast on store, like CPU. 

Against MPSGraph on an M4 Pro, microseconds per call: dense is 2.4x faster below 64K elements (4K 14.1 -> 6.0, 64K 14.3 -> 8.5) and on par from 1M up (35.2 -> 34.8, 16M 984 -> 1003). Broadcast shapes are at parity thanks to the fused-offset kernels two commits down (2D 17.9 -> 19.0, 3D 18.8 -> 19.0), but MPSGraph is still ahead on 4D broadcast (18.4 -> 30.2) and when an operand is transposed (33.9 -> 99.5), where it materializes a tiled copy instead of gathering. Recovering those is follow-up work on the shared family, and would benefit `clamp` and `lerp` too.

title: [MPS] Fix batch_norm aborting on mixed-dtype running stats
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.14.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #198740
* #198739
* #198738

Fixes #154887

`batch_norm` with a half input and float32 running stats -- the ordinary AMP combination, accepted by CPU and CUDA -- killed the interpreter, because MPSGraph fails its module verifier on a mixed operand pair and calls `abort()` rather than throwing.

Narrowing the stats to the input dtype clears both aborts and makes the output, `grad_input` and `grad_bias` match the reference bit-exactly. `grad_weight` is the exception: it is stored at the parameter dtype and the reference computes it there too, so narrowing left it computed in f16 and widened afterwards, a little under 1e-3 off CPU. That one path therefore widens the input to the stats dtype instead, which brings it within a single float32 ulp. The two gradient paths consequently need their epsilon and rsqrt tensors at different dtypes, so the sharing between them is gone and the duplicated version check became a local helper.

The backward also casts `save_mean`/`save_var` on the way in, which costs nothing today because `batch_norm_mps` allocates them at the input dtype. That is deliberate: the reference gives them the parameter dtype when mixed, so ours are arguably wrong, and whoever resolves the standing "Accumulate type?" TODO should not have to fix the backward too.

Training mode is left alone. It never aborted, and its few-ulp difference from CPU is the same TODO -- MPS accumulates batch statistics at the input dtype where the reference uses float. Confirmed pre-existing by reverting this patch and re-running: MPS returns byte-identical values either way. Including it would have forced tolerances loose enough to hide the reinterpretation this is about.

As with the two commits below, OpInfo cannot generate this: every `sample_inputs_*` threads one `dtype` through all operands, so there is no skip to remove either -- the case was never reachable. Hence the hand-written test.

Test Plan:

Both repros from the issue abort before this change and return correct values after:

```
python -c "
import torch
print(torch.nn.functional.batch_norm(
    torch.rand((2, 3, 4), dtype=torch.float16, device='mps'),
    torch.rand((3,), dtype=torch.float32, device='mps'),
    torch.rand((3,), dtype=torch.float32, device='mps')))
"
python -c "
import torch
print(torch.ops.aten._native_batch_norm_legit_no_training.default(
    torch.rand((2, 3, 4), dtype=torch.float16, device='mps'), None, None,
    torch.rand((3,), dtype=torch.float32, device='mps'),
    torch.rand((3,), dtype=torch.float32, device='mps'), 0.1, 1e-05)[0])
"
```

title: Don't import DTensor, FSDP, ONNX and networkx on the torch.compile path
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198752

* #198755

* #198746

A single-process torch.compile imported torch.distributed.tensor (~80ms plus
its op registrations), FSDP, torch.onnx and networkx, although none of them
are used unless the program uses them. The general fix everywhere is the
same: an object can't be a DTensor/FSDP method/ONNX function before its
module has been imported, so checks look the module up in sys.modules
instead of importing it.

Dynamo: variables/functions.py and variables/torch.py imported FSDP's
`_fsdp_param_group` at module level only to compare against
`FSDPParamGroup.use_training_state`. `should_wrap_in_hop` imported
`torch.distributed.tensor.experimental._func_map` on the first traced call.
The EQUALS_MATCH guard imported placement_types for its list of allowed
types. isinstance checks in builder.py, decorators.py and symbolic_shapes.py
spelled `torch.distributed.tensor.DTensor`, which only worked because
something else had imported it; they now use a new
`torch._utils._is_dtensor`. The FSDP guard unpickler imports
`get_cls_to_fsdp_cls` itself since it can run in a fresh process.

Trace rules: `get_torch_obj_rule_map()` resolved every entry of
`torch_name_rule_map` while Dynamo was being imported, importing DTensor
(for `DTensor.from_local`) and torch.onnx. Entries whose module isn't
loaded yet are now kept pending per module and added once the module
appears in sys.modules. Deferring only the polyfill duplicate check was
considered, but tracing calls the same map, so DTensor would just have been
imported during the first compile.

Inductor: inductor_prims imported `_pointwise_ops` to register sharding
strategies for its prims. Now whichever of the two modules is imported

stopped registering the Python-defined symm_mem ops before

imported in the code paths that use them.

Making torch.distributed.tensor cheaper to import was the alternative; it is

for a follow-up.

title: [inductor] Don't wait for the compile sidecar at interpreter exit
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198752
* __->__ #198751
* #198750
* #198755
* #198748
* #198747
* #198746
* #198745

Any process that ran torch.compile spawns the SubprocPool sidecar through
the async-compile warm pool. At exit, the atexit handler (and the
multiprocessing Finalize backup) called `SubprocPool.shutdown()`. That sends
SHUTDOWN and then blocks in `process.wait(300)` until the sidecar exits. For
short runs the sidecar is often still importing torch and booting its worker
pool when the parent finishes, so the parent sat idle for seconds. In the
torchtitan PR53 regional-compile repro, this was about 3s of the ~8s wall
time on a warm cache.

`shutdown` now takes `wait` (default True, so explicit callers are
unchanged). The exit handlers pass `wait=False`: they still send SHUTDOWN and
close the pipe, which the sidecar handles on its own (it also exits on EOF),
but they don't block on it. Pending futures still fail in the `finally`.
Another option was to kill the sidecar outright. That would skip its orderly
teardown of the worker pool and could leak its children, so I didn't do it.

Test Plan:
```
python test/inductor/test_compile_worker.py -k shutdown
python test/inductor/test_async_compile.py
```
The new test_shutdown_no_wait passes. In test_async_compile,
test_pool_method_fork and test_forked_daemon_process_clears_inherited_ready_future
also fail at HEAD on this machine (OMP kmp_affinity abort in forked children).

title: [decomp] Support matmul folding for zero-copy non-contiguous views in torch.compile
body: ## Issue Fixes #197083 ## Summary The Python `matmul` decomposition did not use the same stride check as native `matmul`. It rejected some non-contiguous inputs that can be reshaped without a copy. As a result, `torch.compile` kept the `bmm` path and performed an extra layout copy. This change uses `_compute_stride` for the view check. It also checks `tensor2.mT` when the right-hand input has more dimensions, matching native `matmul`. ## Test Plan - Added tests for: - zero-copy folding with size-1 dimensions; - padded non-contiguous strides; - layouts that cannot be folded; - the higher-rank right-hand-side path using `mT`. - `python -m py_compile torch/_decomp/decompositions.py test/test_decomp.py` - `lintrunner --take FLAKE8,RUFF,PYFMT torch/_decomp/decompositions.py test/test_decomp.py` - `git diff --check` The full PyTorch test suite was not run because this source checkout does not have a local PyTorch build. ## Benchmark Environment: - PyTorch: `2.10.0+cu128` - GPU: NVIDIA A100 - dtype: `float16` - Backend: `torch.compile(inductor)` The following standalone example reproduces the compiled path. Change `B`, `S`, `K`, and `N` to profile other shapes. The example below uses `B=384, S=8192, K=N=4096`. `x[:, :K].unsqueeze(1)` creates the non-contiguous input with stride `(S, K, 1)`. ```python import torch B, S, K, N = 384, 8192, 4096, 4096 class MatmulView(torch.nn.Module): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.weight = torch.nn.Parameter( torch.randn(2, K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16) ) def forward(self, x): lhs = x[:, :K].unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, K], stride [S, K, 1] rhs = self.weight[0] # [K, N], parameter view return torch.matmul(lhs, rhs) x = torch.randn(B, S, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16) model = MatmulView().eval().requires_grad_(False) compiled = torch.compile( model, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, ) with torch.inference_mode(): compiled(x) torch.cuda.synchronize() with torch.profiler.profile( activities=[ torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CPU, torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA, ], record_shapes=True, with_stack=True, ) as prof: compiled(x) torch.cuda.synchronize() print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_cuda_time_total", row_limit=20)) prof.export_chrome_trace("trace.json") ``` These results come from `torch.profiler`. The CUDA column is the matmul kernel self time. Total CPU time includes compiler and runtime overhead and is shown for reference. Before the patch: | Configuration (B/S/K/N) | lhs shape (stride) | bmm CPU time | bmm CUDA kernel | Total CUDA time | Total CPU time | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 16/128/64/128 | (16, 1, 64) (128, 64, 1) | 404.71 μs | 6.94 μs | 6.94 μs | 3.005 ms | | 32/1024/512/512 | (32, 1, 512) (1024, 512, 1) | 315.04 μs | 15.71 μs | 15.71 μs | 2.745 ms | | 64/2048/1024/2048 | (64, 1, 1024) (2048, 1024, 1) | 179.87 μs | 77.98 μs | 77.98 μs | 863.60 μs | | 128/4096/2048/2048 | (128, 1, 2048) (4096, 2048, 1) | 1.246 ms | 258.37 μs | 258.37 μs | 2.908 ms | | 384/8192/4096/4096 | (384, 1, 4096) (8192, 4096, 1) | 624.73 μs | 2.925 ms | 2.925 ms | 4.069 ms | | 512/8192/4096/4096 | (512, 1, 4096) (8192, 4096, 1) | 613.67 μs | 3.897 ms | 3.897 ms | 5.100 ms | After the patch: | Configuration (B/S/K/N) | lhs shape (stride) | mm CPU time | mm CUDA kernel | Total CUDA time | Total CPU time | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 16/128/64/128 | (16, 1, 64) (128, 64, 1) | 223.21 μs | 3.68 μs | 3.68 μs | 2.845 ms | | 32/1024/512/512 | (32, 1, 512) (1024, 512, 1) | 98.48 μs | 5.41 μs | 5.41 μs | 2.279 ms | | 64/2048/1024/2048 | (64, 1, 1024) (2048, 1024, 1) | 85.12 μs | 8.29 μs | 8.29 μs | 781.78 μs | | 128/4096/2048/2048 | (128, 1, 2048) (4096, 2048, 1) | 472.37 μs | 12.54 μs | 12.54 μs | 1.152 ms | | 384/8192/4096/4096 | (384, 1, 4096) (8192, 4096, 1) | 486.37 μs | 61.28 μs | 61.28 μs | 1.205 ms | | 512/8192/4096/4096 | (512, 1, 4096) (8192, 4096, 1) | 405.31 μs | 80.26 μs | 80.26 μs | 939.10 μs | CUDA kernel speedup: | Configuration (B/S/K/N) | Before: bmm | After: mm | Speedup | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 16/128/64/128 | 6.94 μs | 3.68 μs | 1.9x | | 32/1024/512/512 | 15.71 μs | 5.41 μs | 2.9x | | 64/2048/1024/2048 | 77.98 μs | 8.29 μs | 9.4x | | 128/4096/2048/2048 | 258.37 μs | 12.54 μs | 20.6x | | 384/8192/4096/4096 | 2.925 ms | 61.28 μs | 47.7x | | 512/8192/4096/4096 | 3.897 ms | 80.26 μs | 48.6x | The larger configurations benefit most. title: [torch] Add native parallel associative scan (aten::associative_scan)
body:
### Summary

Fixes #95408

Issue #95408 requests a native parallel associative scan to unblock SSM/Mamba and Bayesian-filtering workloads that currently have to hand-roll a custom `torch.func.associative_scan` HOP every time. This PR adds a first-class dispatcher operator `aten::associative_scan` with:

- CPU and CUDA native kernels for the four pointwise builtin combines (`add`, `mul`, `max`, `min`) and the `linear_recurrence` combine that powers the Mamba-style SSM recurrence `h[t] = a[t] * h[t-1] + b[t]`.
- Autograd for `add` (reuses `cumsum_backward`), `mul` (`cumprod_backward`), and `max`/`min` (plateau subgradient).
- An Inductor lowering to `ir.Scan.create` (Triton `tl.associative_scan`) with fallback to the eager native op where scan codegen is unavailable.
- A Blelloch tree decomposition in `torch._decomp` for backends without scan codegen support and for export.
- Routing from `torch.func.associative_scan`: builtin pointwise combines that trace to a single `aten.add/mul/maximum/minimum` are classified at trace time and dispatched to the native kernels; arbitrary combines keep using the generic HOP path.

Semantics match `jax.lax.associative_scan` for the builtin combines (inclusive scan, NaN-propagating max/min).

### Design deviation from a `Callable` schema

`native_functions.yaml` schemas have no callable type, so the op registers a dispatcher-safe `str combine_mode`:

```yaml
- func: associative_scan(Tensor self, str combine_mode, int dim=0, bool reverse=False) -> Tensor
  dispatch:
    CompositeExplicitAutograd: associative_scan

- func: associative_scan.TensorList(Tensor[] xs, str combine_mode, int dim=0, bool reverse=False) -> Tensor[]
  dispatch:
    CompositeExplicitAutograd: associative_scan
```

The `TensorList` overload is the Mamba SSM recurrence over `(a, b)` pairs (`combine_mode='linear_recurrence'`). Arbitrary user combine functions keep working through the existing `torch.func.associative_scan` HOP.

### Key Files Changed

- `aten/src/ATen/native/AssociativeScanKernel.h` — dispatch stubs.
- `aten/src/ATen/native/AssociativeScan.cpp` — op wrappers (movedim/reverse, meta impls), `native_functions.yaml` registrations.
- `aten/src/ATen/native/AssociativeScanUtils.h` — shared `ScanVec`/combine functors (host + device).
- `aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/AssociativeScanKernel.cpp` — work-efficient 2-pass chunked parallel prefix (upsweep + prefix-of-partials + downsweep) over `at::parallel_for`.
- `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/AssociativeScanKernel.cu` — hierarchical block scan: warp-inclusive scan via `__shfl_up_sync`, warp-total scan via shared memory, decoupled look-back over chunks.
- `tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml`, `torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.*` — `associative_scan_backward` (add/mul/max/min).
- `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` — `aten.associative_scan` -> `ir.Scan.create`, fallback to native op when scan codegen is unavailable.
- `torch/_decomp/decompositions.py` — Blelloch tree decomposition.
- `torch/_higher_order_ops/associative_scan.py` — classify builtin combines and dispatch to native op in eager path.
- `test/test_torch.py`, `test/test_autograd.py` — comprehensive operator + autograd tests.
- `benchmarks/associative_scan_bench.py` — correctness + perf harness against eager `cumsum`/`cumprod` and sequential linear-recurrence reference.

### Known Limitations (Initial Version)

- The `TensorList` (`linear_recurrence`) overload has no autograd formula yet; gradient computation for the SSM recurrence is a follow-up.
- `max`/`min` autograd uses the standard subgradient convention (gradient flows to the first element of each constant plateau of the scan output).
- CPU/CUDA only; XPU and MPS are not implemented in this PR.
- Integer dtypes are supported for `add`/`mul` only; `max`/`min` are floating-point (matching jax).

title: [symbolic shapes] Restore exact FloorDiv cancellation
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #198575

Summary

PR [#126905](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/126905) replaced proven-divisible FloorDiv expressions with CleanDiv to preserve integer semantics. However, safe_expand does not simplify C * CleanDiv(x, C) to x. PR [#195383](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195383) exposed this limitation through stricter pattern metadata validation, which rejected equivalent shapes such as x and 2 * (x // 2) even when x % 2 == 0 was known.

This change directly cancels matching factors in C * CleanDiv(x, C) without converting CleanDiv to ordinary division. It supports nested and n-ary products while preserving unmatched CleanDiv expressions.

This restores all 16 vLLM async-TP fusions without requiring vLLM changes.

title: [aarch64] Narrow float/half/bfloat16 -> uint8 via int32 in at::vec::convert
body:
On aarch64, contiguous `x.byte()` for float16/bfloat16 still does a direct `static_cast<uint8_t>`, which clang lowers to a saturating `fcvtzu` (-1 -> 0), while strided copies go through `c10::convert`, which narrows via int64 (-1 -> 255). This breaks `test_non_contig_byte_cpu_{float16,bfloat16}`, `test_contig_vs_every_other_byte_cpu_{float16,bfloat16}` and their `_refs` variants on Apple Silicon (e.g. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/36282025606/job/108516516926). #196646 fixed the same mismatch for float32, but by widening to int64, which on NEON means going through float64 and halves the lane count.

This adds float16/bfloat16 specializations and switches float32 to narrow via int32 instead, using the fact that a type with p significant bits has only multiples of 256 above 2^(p+7): every finite fp16 fits in int32; bf16 is clamped to +-2^16; float32 maps |x| >= 2^31 to 0. All three match `c10::convert` bit for bit wherever it is defined (|x| < 2^63), verified exhaustively for every float16, bfloat16 and float32 bit pattern.

Performance of `x.byte()`, 4M elements, single thread, M5 Pro (us):

 | dtype    | main | this PR |
 |----------|------|---------|
 | float32  | 353  | 294     |
 | float16  | 101  | 172     |
 | bfloat16 | 170  | 281     |

 For reference, a direct (UB) float32 -> uint8 cast takes ~180us, so the defined float32 path is now ~1.6x the plain cast instead of ~2x.

The register-level `VecConvert<uint8_t, 1, float, N>` from #196646 (used by inductor) is left unchanged; it still narrows via int64 and gives identical results.

body:

`torch_key`/`triton_key` hash the torch and triton sources the first time an
FX graph cache key is computed, which blocks the first compile for ~140ms
even on a warm cache. They already support `prefetch()` via
`prefetchable_cache`, but nothing called it.

so the hashing overlaps with everything before the first call (model init,
data loading) as well as Dynamo and AOTAutograd tracing. Dynamo's `_compile`

torch._dynamo.optimize). The prefetchers are bound at codecache import so
tests that `mock.patch` `torch_key` keep working; `TestCacheKeyStrategy`
now clears `triton_key` in setUp because it assumed nothing earlier in the
process had computed the real value.

The cost is importing torch._inductor.codecache inside torch.compile()
instead of inside the first compile, which would have imported it anyway.
Starting only from `_compile` was the first version, but with small
compiled regions Dynamo tracing is too short to hide the hash. Making

title: [export] Fix torch.export.load() failing when called from multiple threads
body:
Fixes #195099

### Problem

`torch.export.load()` fails when two threads load at the same time:

```
AssertionError: _CURRENT_DESERIALIZER is already set
```

### Root cause

`GraphModuleDeserializer.deserialize()` publishes the active deserializer in the module-level global `_CURRENT_DESERIALIZER`, guarded by an assertion that the global is unset and cleared in a `finally`. It is passed this way because `_reconstruct_fake_tensor` is reached through the `FakeTensor` `__reduce__` callback during unpickling and so cannot take it as an argument.

A module global is shared by every thread, so two concurrent loads collide on it and the second one trips the assertion. Subgraphs reuse the enclosing deserializer via `self.deserialize_graph()` rather than re-entering `deserialize()`, so the assertion never fires on legitimate nesting; concurrency is the only way to reach it.

This is the next contention point after #175983, which released the GIL during tensor deserialization and thereby made genuinely parallel loads possible.

### Fix

Make the state a `contextvars.ContextVar` so each thread gets its own binding, and keep the assertion as a per-thread re-entrancy check.

Dropping the assertion instead was considered and rejected: without isolation a second thread would overwrite the first thread's deserializer, and fake tensors would then be reconstructed against the wrong `FakeTensorMode`, turning a loud failure into silent cross-thread corruption. `threading.local()` would also isolate threads but does not carry across async tasks, so the more general primitive is used.

A `ContextVar` is only visible on the thread that set it, unlike the previous global, so this relies on the unpickling running on the calling thread. It does: no part of the load path dispatches to a thread pool, and `deserialize_torch_artifact()` calls `torch.load()` synchronously.

One narrower shared-global race remains on this path: `deserialize()` registers `nn.Module` input types in the process-global pytree registry via `_enable_graph_inputs_of_type_nn_module`, so concurrent loads of programs whose example inputs contain `nn.Module` leaves can still collide. That registry is a separate mechanism and is left for follow-up; plain tensor inputs, as in the reported case, never touch it.

Note that #123789 hit this same assertion from the opposite direction (ExecuTorch wanting recursive deserialization of delegated modules) and proposed making the global a stack; it went stale without review. A stack alone would permit recursion but would still race across threads, so the two concerns are independent. This PR addresses only the threading half; the assertion still rejects same-thread recursion, and a `ContextVar` holding a stack would cover both if recursion is still wanted.

### Test plan

New test, which fails before this change with the reported `AssertionError` and passes after it:

```
python test/export/test_serialize.py TestSaveLoad.test_concurrent_load
```

It loads two differently shaped models across 8 barrier-synchronized threads (via `run_concurrently` from `common_utils`) and checks numerics, so a deserializer leaking between threads is caught rather than just the assertion.

Surrounding suites:

```
python test/export/test_serialize.py     # 131 passed
python test/export/test_serdes.py        # 978 run, 12 pre-existing errors
python test/export/test_cpp_serdes.py    # 479 run, 6 pre-existing errors
python test/export/test_schema.py        # 5 passed
python test/export/test_package.py       # 7 passed
python test/export/test_torchbind.py     # 86 passed
```

The 18 errors in `test_serdes.py` and `test_cpp_serdes.py` are all `test_distributed_*` and `test_export_then_compile_tensor_ctor*`. They reproduce identically with this change reverted and come from a `USE_DISTRIBUTED=0` build and an unrelated inductor codegen failure.

title: [dynamo] Add experimental speculative guard evaluation
body:
> **AI disclosure:** This draft description was prepared with an AI assistant
> and must be reviewed and edited by the author before submission.
>
> ## Summary
>
> This draft adds an experimental, disabled-by-default Dynamo mechanism for
> overlapping cache-entry guard evaluation with execution of a predicted
> backend artifact.
>
> An opted-in backend callable can attach a private speculative descriptor. On
> a cache hit, Dynamo asks the descriptor to launch a transactionally isolated
> artifact, performs the normal complete guard lookup, and commits only if the
> predicted cache entry was selected. A mismatch, cache miss, guard-hook
> rejection, or error aborts the speculative ticket before the normal path
> continues.
>
> Inductor provides an initial conservative implementation for single-device,
> mutation-free CUDA inference graphs. This is a draft for feedback on the
> Dynamo/backend boundary, admission rules, and failure semantics; the feature
> remains off by default.
>
> ## Motivation
>
> Dynamo guard lookup runs before the compiled artifact and can leave an idle
> GPU waiting on latency-sensitive inference. In local Qwen3-8B experiments on
> an NVIDIA A100:
>
> - mutation-free prefill median improved from 20.01 ms to 16.76 ms (16.3%);
> - single-token decode hit median improved from 14.15 ms to 12.95 ms (8.5%);
> - logits and the complete KV cache matched the reference bitwise; and
> - two decode mispredictions cost 26.46 ms and 69.20 ms, demonstrating that
>   hit rate and tail latency are central constraints.
>
> Kineto confirmed that cache lookup ran while the predicted device artifact
> was active. These measurements show available latency headroom, not that the
> mechanism is universally profitable; queued serving can already hide much of
> the same CPU work.
>
> ## Design
>
> - Add private `SpeculationDescriptor.launch()` and
>   `SpeculationTicket.commit()/abort()` protocols, plus a bytecode-resume
>   ticket for backends that produce flattened graph outputs.
> - Propagate an opted-in descriptor through `GuardedCode` into `CacheEntry`.
> - Predict the first backend-compatible entry in normal cache order.
> - Give `launch()` a copy of frame locals, then run the existing cache lookup
>   and guard-complete hook unchanged.
> - Compare the selected and predicted guard managers by retained identity;
>   commit only on an exact match.
> - Re-fetch cache state after arbitrary descriptor code, clear descriptors on
>   invalidation, and preserve primary exceptions and eval-frame state.
> - Keep the ordinary path cheap with an O(1) count of descriptor-bearing
>   entries.
> - Add Kineto ranges for speculative launch, commit, and abort.
> - Let eligible Inductor callables enqueue once, retain private outputs, and
>   hand those outputs to the ordinary Dynamo bytecode after an exact hit. This
>   preserves arbitrary Python output reconstruction.
> - Persist both positive and negative Inductor eligibility decisions through
>   FX and AOTAutograd caches.
>
> Dynamo only captures descriptors for fullgraph, non-export, non-package
> compilations without recorded external Python side effects, backward state,
> or inlined `__torch_function__` subclass dispatch. The backend remains
> responsible for artifact-level safety, including mutation, aliasing, RNG,
> device/stream assumptions, backend specialization, and concurrency.
>
> Inductor currently requires exact direct-local tensor metadata; treats
> weakly held warmed module parameters and buffers as static inputs guarded by
> exact tensor metadata and version; and rejects mutation, RNG, effect tokens,
> CUDA Graph Trees, graph partitions, unsupported source forms, generated
> device assertions, and indirect memory accesses. Commit inserts a CUDA-event
> dependency, while abort synchronizes the event before fallback. Admission is
> checked first on the AOT graph and again after lowering so untagged operations
> such as `aten.gather` are rejected when their generated kernels contain
> indirect memory accesses.
>
> With exact parameter checks enabled, two controlled Qwen prefill runs measured
> 25.88 ms versus 24.10 ms and 21.00 ms versus 19.30 ms (6.9-8.1%). They
> explicitly supplied the model invariant that token IDs were in range.
> Automatic admission rejects Qwen today because `aten.index.Tensor` can
> asynchronously device-assert on a wrong-path launch; the unsafe waiver is not
> part of this diff.
>
> The detailed design and proposed Inductor/KV-cache follow-up are documented
> in
> `docs/source/user_guide/torch_compiler/compile/speculative_guard_evaluation.md`.
>
> ## Feedback requested
>
> - Is a backend-owned launch/commit/abort descriptor the right abstraction?
> - Should admission be split into `prepare()` and `launch()` so launch cannot
>   fail after enqueue but before returning a ticket?
> - Are the initial Dynamo eligibility checks appropriately conservative?
> - Is the two-stage AOT/Inductor admission check the right place to certify a
>   mutation-free, non-faulting artifact?
> - What interface should certify value-domain invariants such as valid token
>   ranges without synchronizing the device before launch?
> - Where should an append-only KV-cache transaction live?
>
> ## Test plan
>
> ```bash
> MAX_JOBS=22 pip install -e . -v --no-build-isolation
> python test/dynamo/test_speculative_guard_eval.py
> python test/inductor/test_speculative_guard_eval.py
> python test/dynamo/test_frame_init.py
> python test/dynamo/test_recompile_ux.py
> python test/dynamo/test_guard_serialization.py
> python test/dynamo/test_config.py
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> The focused build and tests above pass locally (234 tests passed, 2 skipped).
> `spin lint` and `lintrunner -a` could not complete the Python linters because
> the installed `uv` rejects the user-level `uv.toml` `https-proxy` field.
> Clang-tidy also reports pre-existing findings in touched Dynamo C++ files.

title: [inductor] Don't swing a realized buffer in mutate_to
body:
Fixes #198533

`mutate_to`'s fast path replaces the data of the mutated StorageBox with the new value. A realized StorageBox may already be referenced by name: by a ReinterpretView, whose loader looks the name up only when it runs, or by an extern kernel's inputs. Everything lowered before the mutation through those references then reads the new value, including the new value itself. With `y = x + x.sum(-2, keepdim=True)` and a mask of `y.roll(-1, -2) == y.transpose(-1, -2)`, `y.index_put_((mask,), v)` gives wrong values on CPU and CUDA. When an mm reads `y.t()` before the fill, the scheduler fails with a `KeyError`.

The fast path is now taken only for a StorageBox that is not realized. A realized one goes through the existing `realize_into` path, which writes the value into its buffer in place. Inputs, module buffers and NopKernels are all realized nodes, so their three checks are gone. Writing in place means two tensors must not share a buffer:

- A `copy_` node used to give the target its source's buffer, and a later in-place write to either would now change both, so it copies. The values a lowering writes back to a mutated argument (`propagate_mutation`, e.g. after an in-place collective) are still taken as they are, so that code is unchanged.
- An empty buffer that nothing has written yet keeps the fast path, the value copied into its layout, so `empty_like(x).fill_(0)` generates the same code as before.
- `realize_into` no longer uses `unsafe_alias` (the in-place foreach ops) for a realized intermediate, because the foreach value can read it at other positions, as in `_foreach_add_([y], [y.flip(0)])`.

Writing in place also exposes a ConcatKernel bug, found and fixed in #198715: ConcatKernel computes a flexible-layout input straight into the concat buffer, so an in-place mutation of that input after the cat changes the concat. `index_put_` with integer indices after `cat` was already wrong; the masked form was right only because `mutate_to` swung the pointer. The fix is #198715's: GraphLowering collects the fake storages that some node writes in place (including inside control_deps subgraphs), and ConcatKernel copies such inputs instead of computing them into its buffer. `test_cat_input_mutated_after_cat` and the two control_deps tests are from #198715 too.

Test plan, on 2.14 with the change applied at runtime (RTX 4070):

- New tests in test_torchinductor.py: `test_index_put_as_masked_fill_mask_reads_target_view` (wrong values), `..._by_extern_kernel` (`KeyError`), `test_mutate_realized_buffer_in_make_fx_graph` (make_fx graphs that keep `copy_`, `add_` and a foreach flip), `test_cat_input_mutated_after_cat`, and `test_masked_fill_of_realized_buffer_kernel_count`, which checks that a masked fill of an mm output stays one kernel written in place. Halide skips that one: it refuses to fuse a read of the buffer a kernel writes in place, so there the fill is two kernels. All pass on CPU and CUDA in test_torchinductor{,_dynamic_shapes,_codegen_dynamic_shapes}.py and on HalideCpuTests (the kernel-count test skipped, pip halide 21.0.0); without the change 18 of the 30 fail. test_control_deps.py: 13 passed (the two new tests fail without the change).
- `test_inductor_steal_buffer` and the rest of `TestCollectivesInductor` pass (single-rank NCCL), with the same generated code as before; `test_triton_kernel_clone_wekdeps` generates the same code as before, default and cpp_wrapper.
- A/B, same outcome test by test apart from the new tests (about 2,100 tests): the mutation/copy/fill/index_put/cat/concat/scatter/inplace/foreach/alias selections of test_torchinductor{,_dynamic_shapes,_codegen_dynamic_shapes}.py, test_foreach.py, test_inplacing_pass.py, test_auto_functionalize.py, test_triton_kernels.py KernelTests, the cat/stack/index_put/scatter OpInfo tests and TestCollectivesInductor.

Kernels and allocations, before -> after (CUDA; on the C++ CPU backend the same number of kernels or fewer; Halide takes 2 kernels for the masked fill of an mm output):

| Pattern | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `s = x @ w; s.index_put_((m,), -inf)`, and `s[s < 0] = 0` | 1 kernel | 1 kernel |
| fill_, add_ or foreach add_ on a realized mm output, `empty_like(x).fill_(0)`, in-place collectives | same | same |
| `copy_` of an mm output into an empty or unrealized buffer | 0 kernels | 1 kernel |
| `copy_` of an mm output into another realized mm output | 1 kernel, 2 allocations | 2 kernels, 3 allocations |
| foreach add_ into a realized mm output `y` of a value that reads `y` elsewhere (`y.flip(0)`) | 1 kernel | 2 kernels (CPU: 1) |
| A masked fill of a realized buffer whose mask reads that buffer at other positions (`y.roll`) | 2 kernels | 3 kernels (CPU: 1) |

The `copy_` and foreach rows come only from graphs that keep their mutations (make_fx + compile_fx_inner): torch.compile functionalizes them away. In the last row the mask has to be computed before the in-place write.

In that workflow, one GPU captures the model against a fake process group of the serving world size, and then every rank replays the saved artifact with recompilation refused. Each change here was the first blocker at its step: the run got past that step once the change was applied. With the full set, the replay completed on all 16 ranks for 100 batches with no refusals.

**What.** A `CLOSURE_MATCH` on a function, and an `ID_MATCH` on a bound method or a builtin bound to a class, compare object ids. The ids are meaningless in another process, so the serializer refused these guards and the default filter dropped them. When the guarded slot held different functions in different captured variants, the drop was flagged as risky.

At save time, this change rewrites them into by-value checks:
- `FUNCTION_CODE_MATCH`: the function's code object plus the module its globals belong to. Defaults and cells keep their own guards.
- `METHOD_CODE_MATCH`: the same check on a bound method's `__func__`. The receiver is not pinned.
- `NATIVE_METHOD_MATCH`: a builtin bound to a by-reference class, for example an autograd `Function.apply`, compared by equality with `getattr(cls, name)`.

`is_portable_function_guard` lets the precompile default filter keep these guards. A function whose globals no importable module owns is still dropped. The three new guard types are classified as shape-bearing in `precompile_package._SHAPE_BEARING_GUARD_TYPES`, which keeps the guard-policy classification total.

**Why it's needed.** At tip, the strict capture gate refused the model's artifact with 237 risky dropped guards: 236 `CLOSURE_MATCH` on module-level helper functions, and one `ID_MATCH` on an autograd `Function.apply`. title: [inductor] Partition cross-device fallbacks from CUDA graphs
body:
## Summary

> - Split any extern kernel whose FX node reads or produces tensors on more than one device, ignoring meta tensors. This covers `FallbackKernel`, `ExternKernelOut` (custom ops with a `Tag.out` overload), `IndexPutFallback`, and multi-output ops together with their `MultiOutput` children.
> - Keep same-device kernels eligible for CUDA graph capture.
> - Rename and simplify the deterministic `device_put` regression.
> - Add regressions for a CPU-to-CUDA custom op, with and without a `Tag.out` overload, for multi-output ops with a CPU scalar input and with a CPU output, and for `index_put` with CPU indices. Each one checks results against eager and counts the recorded graphs.
> - Add a regression that SDPA with dropout stays in one forward and one backward CUDA graph, so the rule doesn't split attention over the RNG state its backward reads.

## Root cause

CUDAGraph partitions must not read tensor storage allocated outside the active CUDA memory pool. `Scheduler.should_partition` recognized explicit `ir.DeviceCopy` nodes, but a fallback kernel could report a CUDA output device while reading a CPU tensor input. That fallback passed the normal GPU-node check and could be recorded in a CUDA partition, where `check_memory_pool` rejected the CPU storage.

> The scheduler now checks the FX node behind each extern kernel: if the kernel's inputs and outputs span more than one device, it gets its own partition. Deciding on the FX node keeps a multi-output op and its `MultiOutput` children together, the way `is_cudagraph_unsafe_op` already does. Same-device kernels remain eligible for CUDA graph capture. The partition reason is now `cross-device ops`.

Issue #188677 is the earlier CI quarantine of this same regression; #190233 tracks the underlying failure.

Fixes #190233

Fixes #188677

## Test plan

- pre-fix counterfactual: the generic CPU-to-CUDA custom-op regression fails in `check_memory_pool`
- focused device-copy, `device_put`, generic cross-device fallback, and same-device fallback tests pass
- graph-partition subset: 58 passed, 2 skipped
- both positive regressions: 10/10 repeated passes with CUDA memory-leak checking
- `TRITON_OVERRIDE_ARCH=sm86`: both positive regressions pass
- targeted `spin lint` on both changed files, including NEWLINE, Pyrefly, Ruff, Flake8, ClangFormat, and the remaining configured linters
- `git diff --check`

> Re-verified after the FX-level change on an RTX 4080, against torch 2.13 with the rule patched in and Inductor caches disabled, since there was no CUDA build of main. The four new cases crash at record time without the rule and pass with it. A same-device custom op and SDPA forward and backward are not split. Details are in [this comment](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190555#issuecomment-5842853141).
>
> The SDPA dropout test's body was run the same way. It passes with the rule, and fails when the rule sees the seed and offset on the CPU.

ROCm runtime was not available locally, so this PR does not claim ROCm execution coverage.

title: fix compatibility with SciPy >= 1.18 in test_linalg_lstsq
body:
In SciPy >= 1.18, `scipy.linalg.lstsq` migrated to a batched C++ implementation that enforces strict validation on the cutoff condition parameter (`cond >= 0`), raising a `ValueError: Expected rcond >= 0` when passed a negative number. The PyTorch test suite previously passed `rcond=-1` directly to SciPy's reference function when verifying that negative cutoff values instruct underlying LAPACK routines (`gelsd`/`gelss`) to use machine precision tolerance.

To restore compatibility without changing test coverage, this update maps negative `cond` values (such as `-1`) to `None` before calling `scipy.linalg.lstsq` in `check_correctness_scipy`. Because `cond=None` is documented across all SciPy versions to use the default machine precision cutoff threshold, this change maintains backwards compatibility with older versions of SciPy while resolving test failures on SciPy 1.18+.

For reference:
- https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/9392c2abf4de5180c7c125356f0383854611b733

title: Fix index_add_/index_reduce_ docs referring to a src argument
body:
Follow-up to @malfet's review comment on #189008: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/189008#discussion_r3528898334

`Tensor.index_add_` and `Tensor.index_reduce_` both take an argument named `source`, and both docstrings use `source` throughout the prose. Their "output is given as" blocks index a `src` instead, which is not a parameter of either method:

```
index_add_(dim, index, source, *, alpha=1) -> Tensor
    self[index[i], :, :] += alpha * src[i, :, :]  # if dim == 0

index_reduce_(dim, index, source, reduce, *, include_self=True) -> Tensor
    self[index[i], :, :] *= src[i, :, :]  # if dim == 0
```

The `scatter_` / `scatter_add_` / `scatter_reduce_` family a few hundred lines below does take a `src` and uses it correctly, which is where the name looks to have leaked in from.

This renames the six lines to `source`. Docs only, no runtime change. `index_copy_` was checked and is already consistent (it takes `tensor` and its prose and Args both say `tensor`); `torch/_torch_docs.py` has no `src[` occurrences at all, so nothing to change there.

title: [AI Codemod][PerfAICT-General] Memoize wildcard UnionType keys in AliasDb to speed up graph optimization
body:
## Summary

The alias-analysis path (`get_executor` → `optimized_graph` → `preoptimizeGraph` → `PeepholeOptimize`/`ConstantPooling` → `AliasDb`) repeatedly rebuilds `UnionType` instances as keys into `wildcardIndex_`. This memoizes those `UnionType::create` calls so each union key is built at most once per `AliasDb`. 
A new const helper `getWildcardKeyType(type, mut_types)` returns the wildcard index key:

- the **sole mutable type** when there is exactly one, or
- a `UnionType` cached per-`AliasDb` in a new `wildcard_key_types_` map (keyed by
  the declared `TypePtr`) when there are several.

It replaces the `toSingleType`/`UnionType::create` path in
`tryGetOrCreateWildcard` and the inline `UnionType::create` in `getWildcard`.

## Why it's safe

- `UnionType::create` is deterministic and `wildcardIndex_` uses **structural**   hash/equality, so reusing a memoized instance is functionally identical to building a fresh one.
- `toSingleType` is retained for the `Future`/`Await`/`Tuple` mapping paths.
- **No behavior change.**

title: [distributed] Support avg backward for functional reduce_scatter
body:
## Summary

Functional reduce-scatter accepts `avg` in the forward pass, but both its scalar and coalesced autograd paths reject it during backward.

For a group of size `N`, an average reduction contributes a `1 / N` factor to the gradient. The backward is therefore an all-gather of each incoming gradient divided by the group size.

This change:

- permits `avg` in the scalar and coalesced backward paths
- scales incoming gradients by the group size before all-gather
- parametrizes the existing backward tests over `sum` and `avg`

Support for non-`sum` reductions was deferred to a follow-up during #168140.

title: Fix repeat_interleave to preserve channels_last memory format

Fixes:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/65687

`torch.repeat_interleave` does not preserve the input tensor's memory format when dim is specified. A `channels_last` input produces a standard contiguous output, breaking downstream code that relies on format propagation.

**Fix**: When dim is provided, and the input has a non-contiguous memory format (channels_last / channels_last_3d), allocate the output with the correct format upfront and write directly into it, avoiding any extra copy.

title: [inductor] Dump Python stacks on CI test subprocess timeout
body:
Flaky CUDA Inductor tests occasionally hang past 30 minutes and trigger the CI outer timeout. The existing termination path (SIGINT then SIGKILL) yields no diagnostics because processes blocked in native CUDA/Triton code don't act on SIGINT — by the time SIGKILL fires, in-process state is gone.

This PR adds an opt-in SIGUSR1 stack-dump path so test/run_test.py's timeout handler can capture Python stacks from the test subprocess and its Inductor compile workers before the kill sequence runs.

Changes:

1. torch/testing/_internal/common_utils.py
  - install_fault_handler() — enables faulthandler and registers SIGUSR1 to dump every thread's Python stack to the real fd 2 (sys.__stderr__, bypassing pytest's capture proxy). Sets a module-level _fault_handler_installed flag.
  - _dump_subprocess_stacks(pid) — sends SIGUSR1 to pid and all descendants via psutil.Process(pid).children(recursive=True), then sleeps 3s for handler runs / stderr flush. No-ops unless _fault_handler_installed is set, so non-test consumers of wait_for_process don't acquire a SIGUSR1 side effect.
  - wait_for_process — on subprocess.TimeoutExpired, calls _dump_subprocess_stacks(p.pid) before the existing SIGINT/SIGKILL sequence.
2. test/conftest.py
  - pytest_configure calls install_fault_handler() so every pytest subprocess arms the SIGUSR1 handler.
3. torch/_inductor/compile_worker/utils.py
  - _async_compile_initializer installs the same faulthandler/SIGUSR1 registration locally. The default SubprocPool sidecar is started via subprocess.Popen (fresh Python), so the parent's handler does not inherit. SIGUSR1 is otherwise unused in PyTorch.

Result: when the outer timeout fires, the CI log captures Python thread stacks from the test process and every Inductor compile worker, making it possible to identify what's blocking without extending the CI budget.

title: [cuda] Remove host sync from masked_fill_ with a device value tensor
body:
## Summary

`masked_fill_` with a value that lives on the GPU is slower than it needs to be, and it cannot be captured into a CUDA graph.

The CUDA overload reads the fill value with `value.item()`:

```cpp
return masked_fill__cuda(self, mask, value.item());
```

`value.item()` copies one element from the GPU back to the host and blocks the calling thread until the copy lands. So every call with a device value stalls the host. The copy is also illegal during CUDA graph capture, so the op cannot be captured, and it forces a break in `torch.compile` cudagraph regions. You hit this when the fill value came from an earlier GPU computation, for example `x.masked_fill_(mask, scale)` where `scale` is a reduction result still on the device.

This PR reads the value on the GPU instead. For a device value it builds a `TensorIterator` over `self`, the broadcast mask, and the 0-dim value, and a small kernel selects the value where the mask is set. The 0-dim value broadcasts over the output, so there is no host round-trip and the op can be captured.

A CPU value never needed a sync, since `value.item()` there just reads host memory. So a CPU value keeps the old, cheaper path. Only a device value takes the new path, which is the case that used to stall.

The value is cast with `value.to(self.options())` before the kernel runs, so the result matches the existing scalar overload across the supported dtypes. The device, dtype, and overlap checks are preserved.

This follows recent host-sync removals in the CUDA backend, for example #186595 and #189305.

## Test Plan

```
python test/test_torch.py -k test_masked_fill_tensor_value
python test/test_torch.py -k test_masked_fill_tensor_value_cuda_graph
```

I also checked the change on an NVIDIA RTX A4000 (CUDA 12.1). I compiled the exact device-value path as an extension and compared it against the stock op:

- the device-value result matches the scalar overload for float32, float64, float16, bfloat16, and int64
- the stock `masked_fill_(mask, device_value)` fails inside `torch.cuda.graph` capture, while the on-device path captures and replays with the correct result

title: Fix _sympy_mod crash on plain int operands (#198395)
body:
Summary:

# Problem:
f1145204272 failed with error
> InductorError: LoweringException: AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'is_nonnegative'\n  target: <built-in function mod>\n  args[0]: 20\n  args[1]: 8AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'is_nonnegative'\n  target: <built-in function mod>\n  args[0]: 20\n  args[1]: 8

# Proposed fix:

`_sympy_mod` in `torch/fx/experimental/sym_node.py` typed its operands as
`sympy.Basic` and read `.is_nonnegative` off them directly:

```python
def _sympy_mod(a: sympy.Basic, b: sympy.Basic) -> sympy.Basic:
    if a.is_nonnegative and b.is_nonnegative:
        return Mod(a, b)
    else:
        return PythonMod(a, b)
```

That assumption doesn't hold for every caller. `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`
registers a lowering for every entry in `magic_methods` (including
`"mod": _sympy_mod`); when neither operand of `operator.mod` is symbolic or a
`sympy.Basic`, its fallback branch calls the handler directly on the plain
Python scalars instead of routing them through the existing
`_unwrap_symbolic_magic_arg` sympify helper. Plain `int`s don't have
`.is_nonnegative`, so `_sympy_mod(20, 8)` raised
`AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'is_nonnegative'`.

`sympy.Mod`/`PythonMod` themselves would auto-sympify via
`sympy.Function.__new__` if we ever reached them, but the assumption check
runs first and crashes before that happens.

The fix normalizes plain scalar operands with `sympy.sympify` before the
assumption check, mirroring the `(int, float, bool)` normalization already
done in `_unwrap_symbolic_magic_arg`. The type annotation is widened to
`sympy.Basic | int | float | bool` to reflect what the function actually
accepts. The fix is scoped to `sym_node.py` only; `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`
is left untouched.

Added `TestSympyMod` to `test/test_dynamic_shapes.py` covering:
- The exact reported crash: `_sympy_mod(20, 8) == 4`
- Python modulo sign semantics with plain ints: `_sympy_mod(-7, 3) == -7 % 3`
  and `_sympy_mod(7, -3) == 7 % -3` (exercises the `PythonMod` branch)
- Mixed plain-int/sympy operands on either side
- Pre-existing `sympy.Basic` operand behavior is unaffected:

title: [inductor] Skip relational SymBool inputs in Python wrapper
body:
Summary:
## Problem

PT2 traces dynamic tensor dimensions as symbolic shape values. A runtime shape check such as `x.shape[0] <= 128` is input-shape-dependent, not tensor-data-dependent: `x.shape[0]` is a `SymInt` like `s72`, and the comparison is a scalar `SymBool` represented by SymPy as a relational boolean such as `LessThan(s72, 128)`.

This becomes visible when graph partitioning or piecewise compilation exposes that predicate at a graph boundary. One compiled graph can produce or carry `s72 <= 128`, while a later compiled graph receives that predicate as a real FX placeholder and consumes it in `aten._assert_scalar`.

## Solution

Inductor's Python wrapper already handles tensors and numeric symbolic scalar inputs. Numeric `SymInt`/`SymFloat` placeholders are `sympy.Expr` values, and wrapper code may generate local numeric bindings such as `s72 = arg1_1` so later generated Python can use `s72` for allocation, size checks, and stride logic.

A relational `SymBool` input is different. The wrapper still receives and unpacks the graph input, but the relation itself is not a numeric shape symbol that can be assigned. There is no meaningful generated binding like `s72 <= 128 = arg...`; the numeric symbol inside the relation, such as `s72`, is bound separately through the normal `SymInt` or tensor-shape path.

On master, when a relational `SymBool` becomes a compiled graph input, shared wrapper codegen tries to classify it as an input symbol assignment and fails before backend execution with:

```
Unknown value type: <class 'sympy.core.relational.LessThan'>
```

The DeepSeek/MTIA repro hits this with an AOT graph input like `arg11_1: "Sym(s72 <= 262144)"` consumed by `aten._assert_scalar.default(arg11_1, ...)`. Without this change, compilation stops in `codegen_input_symbol_assignment`; with this change, generated Python still unpacks `arg11_1`, emits numeric bindings such as `s72 = arg1_1`, and proceeds through wrapper/kernel generation.

## Change

Teach shared Python wrapper input-symbol codegen to recognize relational `SymBool` inputs represented as SymPy booleans. These inputs are intentionally skipped by `codegen_input_symbol_assignment` because they do not define wrapper-local numeric shape-symbol assignments.

This preserves existing tensor and numeric `SymInt`/`SymFloat` handling while covering the scalar shape-predicate case. The fix belongs in common wrapper code rather than an MTIA-specific wrapper because CPU, GPU, and MTIA can all reach this wrapper failure when a relational `SymBool` predicate crosses a compiled graph boundary.

Tests cover both levels of the behavior: a wrapper-codegen unit test verifies a SymPy relation emits no symbol binding, and a CPU dynamic-shapes regression covers the original `_check`/`_assert_scalar` path plus the reviewer-suggested `int(a)` use. The `keepdim=a` variant is not included because it is rejected earlier by Dynamo/fake tensor validation (`keepdim` must be a concrete bool), before wrapper codegen.

title: Validate lambd in ASGD
body:
### Problem

`ASGD.__init__` validates `lr` and `weight_decay` but not `lambd`. A negative decay term is accepted, and since the update multiplies the parameter by `(1 - lambd * eta)`, a negative `lambd` inverts the decay — the parameter grows instead of shrinking, with no error anywhere:

```python
p = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(3))

ASGD([p], lr=0.1, lambd=1e-4)    # default:  max|param| = 0.9697 after 30 steps
ASGD([p], lr=0.1, lambd=-1e-1)   # negative: max|param| = 1.362   (diverging)
```

### Why this looks like a gap rather than a choice

Every sibling optimizer rejects its analogous parameter:

```
Adam    betas=(-0.1, 0.9)   -> ValueError: Invalid beta parameter at index 0
Adam    eps=-1              -> ValueError: Invalid epsilon value
SGD     momentum=-1         -> ValueError: Invalid momentum value
RMSprop alpha=-1            -> ValueError: Invalid alpha value
Adagrad lr_decay=-1         -> ValueError: Invalid lr_decay value
NAdam   momentum_decay=-1   -> ValueError: Invalid momentum_decay value
Rprop   etas=(-1, 2)        -> ValueError: Invalid eta values
ASGD    lambd=-1            -> accepted
```

I swept the constructors of all of these; `ASGD.lambd` was the only unvalidated one that changes the update's sign.

### Change

Reject `lambd < 0` at construction, following the existing message style in the same file, and add the matching `ErrorOptimizerInput` next to the existing `weight_decay` entry in `common_optimizers.py` so `test_errors` covers it.

`lambd=0` stays valid (it's a legitimate no-decay setting, and the default `1e-4` is unaffected).

### Note on scope

`alpha` and `t0` are also unvalidated. I left them alone deliberately: I couldn't demonstrate a concrete misbehaviour for negative values of either over a short run, and I'd rather not add bounds I can't justify. Happy to extend if you'd like them covered for consistency.

### Testing

```python
ASGD(p, lambd=-1)     -> ValueError: Invalid lambd value: -1
ASGD(p, lambd=-1e-9)  -> ValueError: Invalid lambd value: -1e-09
ASGD(p)               -> ok        (default 1e-4)
ASGD(p, lambd=0.0)    -> ok
ASGD(p, lambd=1.0)    -> ok
```

I'm testing pure-Python changes against a CPU wheel rather than a local build, so CI is the authority for `test_optim`; the new error input follows the existing pattern exactly.

title: [FSDP][AC] Bypass SAC tracking for all-gather internals
body:
Fixes a selective activation checkpointing replay mismatch seen in TorchTitan DeepSeek V3 with FSDP+EP.

TorchTitan tracking issue: https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan/issues/3427

During non-reentrant checkpoint recompute, SAC installs a `TorchDispatchMode` to track ops for replay. FSDP pre-forward hooks may run during that recompute and unshard parameters via all-gather. The all-gather implementation performs communication/materialization internals such as `aten.split_with_sizes.default` and `aten._foreach_copy_.default`; those are not user/model-region ops and may differ between the original forward and recompute.

This introduces an internal SAC bypass context for runtime plumbing regions. SAC caching/replay modes execute ops directly under that bypass without policy calls, storage updates/lookups, or counter increments. FSDP wraps all-gather and copy-out internals in that bypass while preserving the outer FSDP profiler ranges. This keeps unrelated ambient `TorchDispatchMode`s able to observe FSDP internals, unlike a blanket `no_dispatch()` guard.

Profiler `record_function` enter/exit ops are also ignored by SAC because annotations may legitimately differ between forward and recompute and do not produce model values.

The updated regression coverage checks that ambient dispatch modes can still see FSDP all-gather internals, while SAC does not replay-index them. Targeted SAC/FSDP tests and the original TorchTitan repro passed in the H100 validation container.

title: [dynamo] Migrate allow_in_graph → nonstrict_trace in torch/ production code
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack) (oldest at bottom):
* #180616
* __->__ #178416
* #178340

We would like to deprecate allow_in_graph in favor of nonstrict_trace because
they have the same functionality from user's perspecitve i.e. skip dynamo tracing.
They have different unlying implmentations though, nonstrict_trace uses flat_apply HOP
instead of a simple call_function node.

This pr studied what it takes to completely replace allow_in_graph in pytorch. We find 
This migration would require three extensions to nonstrict_trace:

1. in_place kwarg: allow_in_graph registered id(fn) and returned fn
   unchanged. nonstrict_trace by default creates a wrapper. Adding
   in_place=True preserves the old in-place semantics for call sites
   that don't use the return value (einops, bias.py) or need existing
   references to remain recognized by dynamo.

2. Class support: nonstrict_trace wraps via functools.wraps, which
   breaks classes (isinstance, subclassing, attribute access).
   Classes now take the in-place path unconditionally, registering
   id(cls) in _allowed_callable_ids only (not _nonstrict_trace_callable_ids,
   since NONSTRICT_TRACE's flat_apply requires pytree-compatible I/O
   that most classes don't satisfy).

3. SDPAParams as flat_apply leaf: NONSTRICT_TRACE requires outputs to
   be "graphable" (tensors, scalars, etc). SDPAParams isn't pytree-
   registered and failed is_graphable. Rather than requiring pytree
   registration (which is side-effectful), we add register_graphable_type
   to let specific types pass through flat_apply as opaque leaves.
   Also fixed handle_traced_output's SDPAParams branch, which was
   missing the required param_vars argument.

Files changed:
- torch/_dynamo/decorators.py: nonstrict_trace gains in_place kwarg and
  class support; einops registration migrated
- torch/_dynamo/compiled_autograd.py: 3 call sites
- torch/_dynamo/backends/debugging.py: 2 call sites
- torch/compiler/__init__.py: allow_in_graph delegates to nonstrict_trace
- torch/nn/attention/bias.py: 4 call sites + register_graphable_type
- torch/sparse/semi_structured.py: 1 call site
- torch/_higher_order_ops/flat_apply.py: register_graphable_type API
- torch/_dynamo/variables/builder.py: fix handle_traced_output for SDPAParams

The change is kind of substantial with no clear benefits. Given this, should we 
reconsider deprecating allow_in_graph? Maybe we should just keep it as it is
 and creating a cleaner unfied API like https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177180 (which directs to nonstrict_trace or leaf_functino)? @anijain2305 @zou3519

title: RFC : WIP warmup compile with fake tensor with dynamic dims then run with real
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #177283

one possible way to address:

**I want to mark batch size dynamic but  get a single compilation even when there are graph breaks and/or eager code in between compile regions.**

is the following:

Warm up the model first using fake tensors that have dynamic-size inputs, and then run it with real inputs.

why this would work :
1. eager will propagate symbolic shapes of fake tensors. 
2. compile will make dynamic any fake tensor dim that is symbolic. 


Idea :
1. Create a FakeTensor with symbolic batch dimension:
```
# batch dim is symbolic (dynamic), other dims are static
fake_x = create_fake_tensor(shape=[DYNAMIC, 10], device="cuda")
```
2. Run the entire program with FakeTensor:
```
program(fake_x)  # Triggers compilation of ALL graphs
```

- Dynamo traces with symbolic shapes ( a fake tensor with symbolic dim will become dynamic in the input). 
- Eager code propagates dynamism - operations like x + 100, .contiguous() preserve the symbolic shape

3. Run with real tensors - uses cached compiled code:

```
program(torch.randn(32, 10))   # No recompile
program(torch.randn(64, 10))   # No recompile  
program(torch.randn(128, 10))  # No recompile
```
### Issues Faced When Compiling with FakeTensors [can be addressed not blockers ] 


1. C++ Guards crash on symbolic sizes
assert_size_stride and assert_alignment call numel() / storage_offset() which fail on symbolic tensors
Fix: Skip these checks when has_symbolic_sizes_strides() is true
2. Dispatch key mismatch in guards
FakeTensors have Meta dispatch key, but compiled code expects CUDA or CPU
Fix: Skip dispatch key check for FakeTensors, but still verify device type matches
3. Alignment check on FakeTensors
copy_misaligned_inputs checks data_ptr() % ALIGNMENT which crashes on FakeTensors (no real memory)
Fix: Skip alignment check for FakeTensors
4. Generated kernels can't execute with symbolic sizes
Inductor generates code like empty_strided_cuda((s77, 10), ...) - can't allocate real memory with symbolic size
Fix: Short-circuit in CompiledFxGraph.__call__ to run original FX graph instead of generated kernels when FakeTensor detected
5. Recompilation triggered when switching from fake tensor tracing to real tensor execution
Error message: "expected type of 'x' to be a tensor type, but found <class 'torch.Tensor'>"
Root cause: Guard was checking exact Python type (Py_TYPE(value) != _tensor_check->pytype), which failed when FakeTensor ≠ torch.Tensor

title: [MPS] Fix silent corruption in bmm for non-contiguous inputs > 2**32 elements
body:
Fixes #197636.

### Description
This PR addresses a critical bug in the MPS backend where `bmm` silently returns corrupted outputs (and corrupted gradients on the backward pass) when the output exceeds 2**32 elements and the inputs are non-contiguous views (e.g., in eager attention `q @ k.transpose()`). 

**Root Cause:**
When inputs cross the 2**32 element threshold, `bmm_out_mps_impl` routes them to `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl`. However, `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` passes the raw `MTLBuffer` objects directly to `MPSNDArrayDescriptor` without accounting for memory strides. For transposed or sliced inputs, the Metal kernel blindly reads the memory sequentially, causing complete math corruption. 

Because the backward pass calculates gradients using `bmm(G, b.transpose(-1, -2))`, this lack of a `.contiguous()` check also silently corrupts the backward gradients even when the forward pass inputs were perfectly contiguous.

**Fix:**
We explicitly enforce `.contiguous()` on both `batch1` and `batch2` immediately before routing to the `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` function. This forces PyTorch to pack the memory into a row-major layout, allowing the Metal tiled kernel to read the correct values safely and resolving both the forward and backward pass corruptions.

### Testing
- Relying on PyTorch CI for MPS regression test suites.
- Resolves the exact reproduction harness outlined in Issue #197636.

title: [inductor] Fix Triton reduction CSE for logical arg indices
body:
## Summary

Include the logical reduction index in Triton's reduction CSE cache key.

This addresses the remaining Triton cache-key blocker described in #193661 and on #193680: two arg reductions can operate on the same value expression while using different logical index mappings. Caching only by `(src_dtype, reduction_type, value)` can therefore incorrectly reuse one reduction for the other.

The C++ codegen already includes the logical index in its reduction cache key. This change makes Triton follow the same rule.

## Regression

Add focused CUDA/Triton coverage that compiles `x.argmax()` and `x.t().argmax()` in the same graph. They share the same underlying values but require different logical indices, directly exercising the reduction-CSE collision.

## Context

This PR previously targeted the narrower adaptive-average-pool symptom from #193492. That issue was closed in favor of the broader logical-vs-physical reduction indexing problem in #193661. The branch is repurposed to address the explicit Triton CSE blocker for the broader fix in #193680.

Related: #193661
Unblocks: #193680

## Validation

- `python -m py_compile torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py test/inductor/test_triton_reduction_cse.py`
- `git diff --check`

Both checks completed successfully on the branch update runner. Full GPU regression coverage is left to PyTorch CI.

title: Fix uninitialized memory warnings in CPU linear algebra kernels
body:
Modifies ATen CPU linear algebra kernels in `BatchLinearAlgebraKernel.cpp` to value-initialize workspace query variables and `.zero_()` output tensors before passing their buffers to external BLAS/LAPACK functions.

When building PyTorch with MemorySanitizer (`msan`), test suites executing CPU linear algebra operations (such as `torch.linalg.svd`, `cholesky`, `qr`, and` lu_factor`) fail with false-positive `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` errors.

This occurs due to two distinct patterns when interacting with external BLAS/LAPACK libraries (e.g., MKL, OpenBLAS, Netlib LAPACK):

1. **Optimal workspace size queries**: When querying LAPACK routines for optimal workspace sizes (`lwork = -1`), local floating-point variables (e.g., `wkopt`, `work_query`) were passed by pointer uninitialized. Because external precompiled BLAS/LAPACK libraries are uninstrumented under MSan, writes to `&wkopt` do not update MSan shadow memory. When 
`lapack_work_to_int` subsequently invokes `std::nextafter()` on the returned value, MSan checks shadow memory and triggers an error.
2. **Computational outputs**: Output tensors allocated via structured kernels or `at::empty()` start with uninitialized memory and uninitialized MSan shadow memory. When uninstrumented LAPACK computation routines populate these buffers, shadow memory remains marked uninitialized. Subsequent tensor operations or test comparisons (e.g., ``at::isnan()`) trigger uninitialized storage exceptions.

### Changes

- `BatchLinearAlgebraKernel.cpp`:
  - Value-initialized scalar workspace query variables (`work_query = 0`, `lwork_query = 0`, `rwork_query = 0`, `wkopt = 0`, `work_opt = 0`, `rwork_opt = 0`) across all LAPACK query sites (`lapackEig`, `lapackSyevd`, `lapackGeqrf`, `lapackOrgqr`, `lapackOrmqr`, `lapackLdl*`, `lapackSvd`).
  - Added zero initialization calls (`.zero_()`) for output tensors in Cholesky, LU factorization, and SVD kernels before passing their underlying data pointers to BLAS/LAPACK routines.
- `ts_native_functions.cpp`:
  - Added 0-dimension tensor zeroing in `empty_symint` to prevent MSan failures when hashing newly initialized lazy scalar tensors during device data caching.

title: Fix LayerNorm returning non-zero on constant input
body:
## Issue

Fixes #198581

Supersedes #198587 (auto-closed when its head fork was deleted). Same commit, same diff.

## Summary

- `cuWelfordCombine` merged two partial means as a weighted average, `nA*dataA.mean + nB*dataB.mean`, which is exact only when `nA + nB == 1` - something no reciprocal guarantees. On constant input the saved mean came back one ulp low and `rsqrt(eps)` amplified it, so `F.layer_norm(torch.ones(4, 384), (384,), eps=1e-5)` returned `1.88e-05` on gfx950 instead of `0`.
- Replaced with Welford's increment, `dataA.mean + delta * nB`, which cannot move the mean when both partials agree, whatever the reciprocal did. This matches `WelfordOps::combine` in `SharedReduceOps.h`, already used by `torch.mean` and by LayerNorm's own `N % 4 != 0` fallback.
- Making the reciprocal exact instead is measurably not a fix: with correctly-rounded `1.0f/count` the old formula still fails 131 of 1024 widths on hardware. Only the formula change gives 0.
- Measured on MI355X (gfx950) and MI300X (gfx942); the failure and the saved-mean bit patterns are identical on both, and reproduce as far back as torch 2.7.1+rocm6.4.1. The CUDA block shape is covered by arithmetic reasoning, not by execution.

## Checklist

- [x] Passes lint (`lintrunner -a aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu test/test_nn.py`)
- [x] Added/updated tests
- [ ] Updated documentation (not applicable)
- [x] Included benchmark results

## BC-breaking?

No API change. It does change bitwise forward output for non-constant input on every GPU backend, since `mA + delta*nB` and `nA*mA + nB*mB` round differently - the new form is the better-conditioned one and is what the rest of ATen already uses. Tolerance-based suites pass on gfx950 (`test_nn.py -k LayerNorm` 50, `-k rmsnorm` 12, `test_ops.py -k layer_norm` 164).

<details>
<summary>Detailed analysis, measurements and test plan (produced with Claude Code)</summary>

> ## Summary
>
> `cuWelfordCombine` in the vectorized LayerNorm kernel merges two partial means as a weighted average, `nA*dataA.mean + nB*dataB.mean`, which is exact only when `nA + nB == 1` — something no reciprocal guarantees. On a constant input, where the mean must be exact for the output to be zero, this makes `F.layer_norm` return non-zero. This replaces it with Welford's increment, `dataA.mean + delta * nB`, which is exactly mean-preserving when both partials agree. Fixes #198581.
>
> ## What changed
>

> F.layer_norm(x, (244,), eps=1e-5).abs().max()   # predicted non-zero
> ```
